title: Given a set of distinct elements, generate all possible subsets, also called the power set, using backtracking.
shortTitle: Generate All Subsets of a Set (Backtracking / Power Set)

s1_definition.profdef: The power set of a set is the collection of all its subsets, including the empty set and the full set, and a set of n elements has exactly two to the power n subsets. Backtracking generates them by walking the elements in order and, at each element, exploring two branches: include it or exclude it. Each complete path from start to end corresponds to one subset. The algorithm runs in time proportional to n times two to the n because it builds that many subsets.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India offers n optional add-on services on an account, and wants to list every possible combination a customer could choose, from choosing nothing to choosing everything. A clerk goes through the add-ons one at a time, and for each one she branches into two worlds: one where the customer takes it and one where they skip it. By the time she has decided on all add-ons, each distinct sequence of take-or-skip choices is one possible package. Listing every such sequence gives every possible package.
s1_definition.oneliner: For each element choose include or exclude; every complete choice sequence is one subset, giving two to the n subsets.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The power set of a set is the collection of all its subsets, including the empty set and the full set, and a set of n elements has exactly two to the power n subsets. Backtracking generates them by walking the elements in order and, at each element, exploring two branches: include it or exclude it. Each complete path from start to end corresponds to one subset. The algorithm runs in time proportional to n times two to the n because it builds that many subsets.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India offers n optional add-on services on an account, and wants to list every possible combination a customer could choose, from choosing nothing to choosing everything. A clerk goes through the add-ons one at a time, and for each one she branches into two worlds: one where the customer takes it and one where they skip it. By the time she has decided on all add-ons, each distinct sequence of take-or-skip choices is one possible package. Listing every such sequence gives every possible package.

**One line to remember:** For each element choose include or exclude; every complete choice sequence is one subset, giving two to the n subsets.

sections.s2_technical:
Backtracking is a disciplined depth-first exploration of a decision tree where you build a partial solution, recurse to extend it, then undo the last choice to try alternatives. For subsets the decision at each step is simply whether to include the current element.

The common formulation uses a start index and a running list. At every call you first record the current running list as a valid subset, because every prefix of choices is itself a complete subset. Then you loop from the start index to the end, and for each index you add that element to the running list, recurse with the next index, and then remove the element to backtrack. That add, recurse, remove rhythm is the heart of backtracking: `path.add(nums[i]); backtrack(i + 1); path.remove(path.size() - 1);`. The removal restores the state so the next iteration explores a different branch cleanly.

A subtle but important point is passing a copy when you record a subset, for example `result.add(new ArrayList<>(path));`, because the running list is mutated throughout; if you stored the reference directly, every stored subset would later reflect the final mutated state. Starting the loop at the current index rather than zero prevents generating the same subset in different orders, so you get each subset once.

A senior-level nuance is that there are two other classic ways to produce the power set. The iterative "cascade" starts with the empty subset and, for each element, adds that element to copies of all existing subsets, doubling the count each round. The bitmask method iterates an integer from zero to two-to-the-n minus one and treats each bit as include-or-exclude, which is extremely compact. All three are equivalent; backtracking generalises best to constrained variants like subsets with a size limit or no duplicates, which is why interviewers favour it.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India bundles optional account add-on services, and the pricing and marketing teams need the full list of every possible combination to price and present each package. This is exactly the power set, generated by including or excluding each add-on.

Problem 2 — Each package must be distinct and must appear exactly once, including the empty package where the customer chooses nothing. The start-index backtracking guarantees no subset is produced twice and that the empty subset is included.

In our mini-project we build an `AddonPackager` that returns all subsets of a list of add-on codes using backtracking. The demo generates all packages from three add-ons and logs them.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: three add-ons, SMS alerts, insurance, overdraft, generating all packages.

Step 1: Enter backtrack at start zero with an empty path. We record the empty path as the first package, the empty package where the customer takes nothing.

Step 2: Loop from index zero. Add SMS alerts, recurse at start one. Inside, record the path containing SMS alerts.

Step 3: Still inside, loop from index one. Add insurance, recurse at start two, record SMS alerts plus insurance. Loop from index two, add overdraft, recurse at start three, record SMS alerts plus insurance plus overdraft, then backtrack by removing overdraft, then backtrack by removing insurance.

Step 4: Back at the SMS-alerts level, continue the loop to index two. Add overdraft, recurse, record SMS alerts plus overdraft, backtrack removing overdraft, then backtrack removing SMS alerts.

Step 5: Back at the top level, continue to index one. Add insurance, recurse, record insurance; inside add overdraft, record insurance plus overdraft; backtrack. Continue to index two, add overdraft, record overdraft.

Step 6: Every branch has been explored and undone. The result holds all eight packages, exactly two to the power three, each distinct and including the empty one. Each stored subset is an independent copy, so none reflects later mutations.

```
[2026-10-26 23:32:01] INFO    Total packages: 8
[2026-10-26 23:32:01] INFO      package: []
[2026-10-26 23:32:01] INFO      package: [SMS_ALERTS]
[2026-10-26 23:32:01] INFO      package: [SMS_ALERTS, INSURANCE]
[2026-10-26 23:32:01] INFO      package: [SMS_ALERTS, INSURANCE, OVERDRAFT]
[2026-10-26 23:32:01] INFO      package: [SMS_ALERTS, OVERDRAFT]
[2026-10-26 23:32:01] INFO      package: [INSURANCE]
[2026-10-26 23:32:01] INFO      package: [INSURANCE, OVERDRAFT]

```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  addons: [SMS, INS, OVD]   decision tree (include→right branch)

  []                                   ← record at every node
  ├─ SMS
  │   ├─ SMS,INS
  │   │   └─ SMS,INS,OVD
  │   └─ SMS,OVD
  ├─ INS
  │   └─ INS,OVD
  └─ OVD

  add → recurse(i+1) → remove (backtrack)   → 2^3 = 8 subsets
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The power set is the collection of all subsets of a set, including the empty set and the full set, and a set of n elements has exactly two to the power n subsets. I generate them with backtracking, which is a disciplined depth-first walk of a decision tree where at each element I branch into two possibilities: include it or exclude it. Every complete sequence of include-or-exclude decisions corresponds to exactly one subset.

In code I use a start index and a running path list. At the start of every recursive call I record the current path as a valid subset, because every prefix of choices is itself a complete subset, and that is how the empty subset gets captured at the very first call. Then I loop from the start index, and for each element I add it to the path, recurse with the next index, and remove it to backtrack. That add, recurse, remove rhythm is the essence of backtracking, and the removal restores state so the next branch is explored cleanly. One detail I am always careful about is storing a copy of the path when I record a subset, because the path is mutated throughout, so storing the reference directly would make every stored subset reflect the final state.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to enumerate add-on service packages, where optional services can be combined in any way, and the pricing and marketing teams needed every possible combination from the empty package to the full one. The start-index approach guaranteed each package appeared exactly once and that the empty package was included.

The senior-level point I make is that there are three equivalent ways to build a power set: this backtracking approach, an iterative cascade that doubles the subset list for each element, and a bitmask method that treats the bits of an integer from zero up to two-to-the-n as include flags. They all produce the same result, but I prefer backtracking because it generalises cleanly to constrained variants, such as subsets of a fixed size or subsets of a multiset with duplicates, where I add a small pruning or skip condition to the same skeleton.
